title: A Demonstration in Tokyo
bigQuestion: How did an art from the Ryukyu Islands become a karate school in Tokyo and a storefront sign around the world?

story.title: An Empty Floor in Tokyo
story.kicker: In 1922, a schoolteacher from Okinawa brought his home island's art to Japan's capital.
paragraphs: It is May 1922 in Tokyo. Japan's Ministry of Education is holding a big national exhibition about sport and physical education. Teachers from many parts of Japan have come to show their work.

One visitor is Funakoshi Gichin. He is a quiet schoolteacher from Shuri, on the island of Okinawa. He studied the art as a boy. He has come to show an art his island calls tōde, a word that means "Tang hand" or "China hand."
Most people in Tokyo have never seen this art. Okinawa is far to the south. It was once its own kingdom, called Ryukyu. Japan made it a prefecture, or state, only 43 years earlier, in 1879.

People notice the demonstration. Soon Kanō Jigorō, the founder of judo, invites Funakoshi to show the art at the Kodokan, the judo school. Funakoshi stays. He spends most of the rest of his life on mainland Japan, teaching.
The art he brought would get a new name, new ranks and new rooms. Decades later, the word karate would hang over shop doors in the United States. This chapter tells how that happened.
story.think: Why might a teacher decide to stay far from home to share an art?

lessons.title: The Ryukyu Kingdom
lessons.mainIdea: Before it was part of Japan, Okinawa was the center of the Ryukyu Kingdom, a trading nation with its own king.
reading: The *Ryukyu* Islands are a chain of islands between Japan and Taiwan. Okinawa is the biggest one. In 1429, a leader named Shō Hashi joined the island's three small kingdoms into one. It became the Ryukyu Kingdom.

The kings lived at Shuri Castle, on a hill above the port of Naha. Ryukyu ships sailed to China, Korea, Japan and Southeast Asia. They traded goods like cloth, pottery, spices and horses. The kingdom grew rich as a go-between for many ports.

From 1372, Ryukyu sent *tribute* to the emperors of China. Tribute meant gifts and visits that showed respect for a stronger ruler. In return, China allowed trade. Shuri Castle burned in a fire in 2019, and Okinawa is rebuilding it.

words.d: the chain of islands that includes Okinawa; also the name of the kingdom there from 1429 to 1879
gifts and visits a smaller kingdom sent to a stronger ruler to show respect and keep trade open

lessons.title: Neighbors from Fujian
lessons.mainIdea: Chinese families living in Okinawa, and Okinawans who traveled to China, carried Chinese fighting arts to the islands.
reading: Near Naha was a village called *Kume*. Chinese families lived there, many from the province of *Fujian* in southern China. Tradition says the first families came in 1392. The people of Kume worked as writers, translators and ship pilots for the kingdom.

Okinawans also traveled to China. Students and officials sailed to the city of Fuzhou, in Fujian. Some stayed for years. In the late 1800s, a man from Naha named Higaonna Kanryō studied a Chinese art in Fuzhou and taught it after he came home.

Historians agree that Chinese arts shaped Okinawan fighting arts. They do not agree on every detail. Few written records survive from before the 1800s. Much of what we know came from teachers passing stories to students.

words.d: a village near Naha where Chinese families lived and worked for the Ryukyu Kingdom
a province on the southern coast of China; its city Fuzhou had close ties to Ryukyu

look.title: A Ship Between Two Ports
look.text: Picture a Ryukyu ship leaving Naha in the 1800s. It carries officials, students, letters and gifts for the Chinese court. It is sailing west toward Fuzhou. Some of the young men on board will stay in China for years before they sail home.
look.prompt: What kinds of things, besides goods, might travel home on a ship like this?

check.why: Many Kume families came from Fujian, a province in southern China.

lessons.title: Te and Tōde
lessons.mainIdea: Before the word karate was common, Okinawans used older names such as te and tōde, and named styles after their towns.
reading: Okinawans had an old word for their fighting art: *te*. It simply means "hand." Another name was *tōde*. It means "Tang hand." Tang was an old name for China, after the Tang dynasty. So tōde meant a hand art from China.

People also named the art after towns. Shuri-te came from Shuri, the royal capital. Naha-te came from the port of Naha. Tomari-te came from the village of Tomari. Each town had its own teachers and its own ways.

The written form of tōde used two Chinese characters. The same two characters could also be read aloud as "karate." So the word karate first meant "China hand," not "empty hand." That meaning changed later, in the 1930s.

words.d: an old Okinawan word for the fighting art; it means hand
an older name for the art; it means Tang hand, or China hand

look.title: Three Towns, Three Names
look.text: Shuri-te: named for Shuri, where the king lived. Naha-te: named for Naha, the busy port. Tomari-te: named for Tomari, a village between them. All three are on the same island, only a few miles apart.
look.prompt: Why might people name an art after a town instead of a person?

check.q: What does the Okinawan word te mean?
check.why: Te is an old Okinawan word that means hand.

check.q: What did tōde mean?
check.why: Tōde meant Tang hand. Tang was an old name for China.

check.q: Where did the name Naha-te come from?
check.why: Naha-te was named for the port of Naha. Shuri-te and Tomari-te were named for towns too.

lessons.title: Japan Takes Okinawa
lessons.mainIdea: Japan's Satsuma domain invaded Ryukyu in 1609, and Japan made the kingdom into Okinawa Prefecture in 1879.
reading: In 1609, soldiers from Satsuma invaded Ryukyu. Satsuma was a domain, or region, in southern Japan. After the invasion, Ryukyu had to obey Satsuma. It still sent tribute to China too. The kingdom now answered to two powers.

In 1879, the government of Japan ended the kingdom. It made Ryukyu into *Okinawa Prefecture*. A prefecture is like a state. The last king, Shō Tai, was moved to Tokyo. Schools began teaching in Japanese instead of the Okinawan language.

A popular story says Okinawans built their empty-hand arts because rulers banned weapons. Historians call this story too simple. Weapon rules did exist, but the arts grew from many sources, including trade and teachers from China.

words.d: a region of old Japan ruled by a lord; Satsuma was one
the Japanese state created from the Ryukyu Kingdom in 1879

look.title: A Story and a Record
look.text: Story: "People on Okinawa invented fighting with empty hands because swords were banned." Record: Ryukyu traded with China for centuries, Chinese families lived in Kume, and Okinawans studied in Fuzhou.
look.prompt: Which is easier to check with records, the story or the list of facts? Why?

check.why: Soldiers from the Satsuma domain invaded Ryukyu in 1609.

check.q: What happened in 1879?

check.why: In 1879, Japan ended the kingdom and created Okinawa Prefecture.

check.q: What do historians say about the weapon-ban story?
choices: It is written in the Olympic rules

check.why: Historians say the arts grew from trade, Chinese teachers and more, not only a ban.

lessons.title: Itosu Brings It to School
lessons.mainIdea: In the early 1900s, the teacher Itosu Ankō helped bring karate into Okinawa's public schools as exercise for students.
reading: Itosu Ankō lived from 1831 to 1915. He was a teacher from Shuri. Around 1901, he helped bring the art into Okinawa's schools. Until then, teachers often taught a few students in private, in yards or homes.

In school, the art changed. Large groups of students practiced together. Teachers used it as *physical education*, a school subject that builds health and strength. Itosu made new, simpler training patterns for children.

In 1908, Itosu wrote a letter to Okinawa's school leaders. It listed ten short lessons about the art. People often call it Itosu's *precepts*. The letter said the art was good for health and should help people avoid fights.

words.d: a school subject that builds health and strength through exercise
short rules or lessons for how to act

look.title: Itosu's Letter, 1908
look.text: This art is not only for your own good. It can help protect your family. It is meant to avoid a fight, not to start one. Practiced from childhood, it builds strong bodies.
look.cite: Itosu Ankō, letter of ten precepts to the Okinawa Prefecture education office, 1908
look.prompt: What reasons does Itosu give for teaching the art to students?

check.q: About when did karate enter Okinawa's schools?
check.why: Itosu Ankō helped bring the art into schools around 1901.

check.q: What are precepts?
choices: short rules or lessons for how to act
check.why: Itosu's 1908 letter listed ten precepts, or short lessons.

check.q: How did teaching change when the art entered schools?
choices: It was taught only at night in secret
Large groups practiced together as physical education
check.why: In school, large groups practiced together, and teachers used it to build health.

lessons.title: Funakoshi Goes to Tokyo
lessons.mainIdea: In 1922, Funakoshi Gichin demonstrated the Okinawan art in Tokyo and stayed to teach it in Japan's capital.
reading: Funakoshi Gichin was born in Shuri in 1868. He studied with Itosu Ankō and another Shuri teacher, Azato Ankō. For many years, he worked as a schoolteacher in Okinawa.

In 1922, Funakoshi showed the art at a national exhibition in Tokyo. The Ministry of Education ran the event. That same year, Kanō Jigorō invited him to demonstrate at the Kodokan. Kanō was the founder of judo and a leader in Japanese education.

Funakoshi stayed in Tokyo. He first lived and taught at a *dormitory*, a building where students live, for young men from Okinawa. In 1922 he also published his first *book* on the art. He wrote it for readers in mainland Japan.

words.d: a building where students live together
Funakoshi's first book on the art, Ryūkyū Kenpō Karate, printed in Tokyo in 1922
a public showing of how something is done, so others can see it

look.title: Two Teachers Meet
look.text: Kanō Jigorō had turned older jujutsu schools into judo, with ranks, a rule book and a school, the Kodokan. Funakoshi Gichin came from Okinawa with an art taught mostly by one teacher to a few students. In 1922, Kanō invited Funakoshi to show it at the Kodokan.
look.prompt: What might Funakoshi have learned from seeing how Kanō organized judo?

check.why: Funakoshi was born in Shuri, Okinawa, in 1868.

check.q: What did Funakoshi do in 1922 besides his demonstration?
choices: published his first book on the art
check.why: In 1922, Funakoshi published his first book, written for readers in mainland Japan.

lessons.title: China Hand to Empty Hand
lessons.mainIdea: In the 1930s, teachers changed how karate was written so that it meant empty hand instead of China hand.
reading: At first, karate was written with characters meaning "China hand." In the late 1920s and 1930s, teachers in Tokyo began to write it another way. The new first character meant "empty." It sounded the same, but now karate meant *empty hand*.

Funakoshi's 1935 book, Karate-dō Kyōhan, used the new writing. At that time, Japan and China were in growing conflict. Some teachers wanted a name that sounded Japanese. Others liked that "empty" also had a meaning in Buddhist thought.
On October 25, 1936, Okinawan teachers met in Naha. A local newspaper hosted the meeting. The teachers agreed to use the new name. Today, Okinawa Prefecture marks October 25 as *Karate Day*.

words.d: the meaning of karate after the 1930s, when the first character changed from China to empty
October 25, marked in Okinawa to remember the 1936 meeting on the name

look.title: Same Sound, New Meaning
look.text: Before: kara-te, written with characters meaning "China" and "hand." After: kara-te, written with characters meaning "empty" and "hand." When you say it aloud, both sound exactly the same. Only the writing changed.
look.prompt: Why might changing just the writing of a name matter to people in 1936?

check.q: What did karate come to mean after the 1930s?
check.why: The first character changed to one meaning empty, so karate came to mean empty hand.

check.q: What happened in Naha on October 25, 1936?
choices: Okinawan teachers agreed to use the new name
check.why: At a meeting in Naha, Okinawan teachers agreed on the empty-hand name.

check.q: Why did some teachers want a new way to write the name?
choices: Japan and China were in growing conflict
The old name was too long
check.why: Japan and China were in conflict, and some teachers wanted a name that sounded Japanese.

lessons.title: Clubs, Belts and Jackets
lessons.mainIdea: In Tokyo, karate borrowed judo's white jacket and dan ranks and grew in university clubs.
reading: In Tokyo, karate began to look more like judo. Funakoshi borrowed the white cotton jacket and pants. He also borrowed judo's *dan* ranks. A dan is a numbered black-belt rank. Beginners held lower ranks called kyū.

University students joined in. Keio University started a karate club in 1924. Clubs soon formed at other Tokyo universities. A *university club* is a student group with its own members, officers and teacher. Clubs held meets and demonstrations with each other.

In 1939, Funakoshi's students built him a dojo in Tokyo. It was called the Shōtōkan, the hall of Shōtō. Shōtō was the pen name Funakoshi used for his poems. The building was destroyed by bombing in 1945, during World War II.

words.d: a numbered black-belt rank; karate borrowed the dan system from judo
a student group at a college with its own members, officers and teacher
Funakoshi's dojo in Tokyo, opened in 1939; later the name of a karate style

look.prompt: Why might a new art in Tokyo borrow the look of an art people already knew?

check.why: A dan is a numbered black-belt rank. Karate borrowed dan ranks from judo.

check.q: Which university started a karate club in 1924?
check.why: Keio University in Tokyo started a karate club in 1924.

check.q: Where did the name Shōtōkan come from?
choices: Shōtō, Funakoshi's pen name for his poems
check.why: Shōtōkan means the hall of Shōtō, the pen name Funakoshi used.

lessons.title: Many Schools of Karate
lessons.mainIdea: Karate split into many named schools, called ryū, each tied to a founder and a place.
reading: Japanese uses the word *ryū* for a school or style. By the 1930s, karate had several ryū. Gōjū-ryū came from Miyagi Chōjun of Naha. Gōjū means "hard and soft." Shōrin-ryū grew from the teachers of Shuri.

Some schools began on mainland Japan. Ōtsuka Hironori had studied jujutsu and then trained with Funakoshi. He started Wadō-ryū, the "way of harmony." Mabuni Kenwa, from Okinawa, moved to Osaka and started Shitō-ryū.

After World War II, groups formed to link many dojos. The *Japan Karate Association* began in Tokyo in 1949. It gave ranks and trained teachers. Funakoshi died in 1957. Many groups, not one, now claim parts of his teaching.

words.d: a Japanese word for a school or style, such as Gōjū-ryū or Wadō-ryū
a karate organization founded in Tokyo in 1949 that gave ranks and trained teachers

look.title: Four Schools, Four Places

look.prompt: Which schools started on Okinawa, and which started on mainland Japan?

check.why: Ryū means a school or style, as in Gōjū-ryū.

check.q: Who founded Gōjū-ryū?
check.why: Miyagi Chōjun, a teacher from Naha, founded Gōjū-ryū.

check.q: When did the Japan Karate Association begin?
check.why: The Japan Karate Association began in Tokyo in 1949.

lessons.title: Soldiers and Storefronts
lessons.mainIdea: After 1945, American service members learned karate in Okinawa and Japan and opened schools back home.
reading: World War II ended in 1945. The United States ran Okinawa until 1972, much longer than the rest of Japan. Large American bases stood on the island. Many American service members studied at Okinawan dojos near the bases.

When they went home, some opened karate schools. By the 1960s, schools stood in *storefront* rooms, shops facing the street, in many American towns. The word karate became famous through these schools and through movies and TV.

Soon the word stretched. Many Korean teachers in America put "Korean karate" on their signs because Americans knew the word. Chinese arts were sometimes sold as karate too. To many Americans, karate became a *catch-all* word for any art from East Asia.

words.d: a shop room that faces the street; many American karate schools opened in them
a word used for many different things, even when they are not the same

look.title: Three Signs on One Street
look.text: Picture a street in an American town in the 1960s. One sign says "Okinawan Karate." Another sign, down the block, says "Korean Karate." A third says "Karate and Kung Fu." Each school teaches an art from a different place.
look.prompt: Why might three different teachers all use the word karate on their signs?

check.why: The United States ran Okinawa after World War II until 1972.

check.q: Why did some Korean teachers in America use the words Korean karate?

check.why: Americans knew the word karate, so it helped people find the school.

lessons.title: Karate at the Olympics
lessons.mainIdea: Karate was an Olympic sport once, at the Tokyo 2020 Games held in 2021, and an Okinawan won gold.
reading: Karate's world sport group is the *World Karate Federation*. It grew from a group formed in 1970. The IOC, the International Olympic Committee, recognized it in 1999. It writes the rules for karate matches around the world.

In 2016, the IOC added karate for the Tokyo 2020 Games. The Games were delayed a year by the COVID-19 pandemic and held in 2021. Karate took place at the Nippon Budokan, a famous hall in Tokyo. There were two kinds of events: *kata*, judged routines, and kumite, matches.

Kiyuna Ryō, from Okinawa, won the men's kata gold medal. Sandra Sánchez of Spain won the women's kata gold. Karate was not kept for the Paris 2024 Games. So far, Tokyo is the only Olympics with karate medals.

words.d: the world group that writes karate competition rules; recognized by the IOC in 1999
a set routine performed alone and judged; one of the two kinds of Olympic karate events
the International Olympic Committee, which decides which sports are in the Olympics
